# Innovation Capacity & Experimentation Initiative
## Companion paper to the Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 1.0 — for decision at the sponsor group meeting of 18 March, alongside Empowerment v2.0. For prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads, the four regional MDs, and — new to this paper — the regional heads of product, operations and commercial. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

Two notes, and then the substance.

**The first is a recommendation the sponsor group may not expect from us: this should probably not be a second programme.** It arrives as one because it was commissioned as one. But a region that receives two centrally-authored culture initiatives inside a single financial year will, quite reasonably, treat the second as evidence that the first was not serious. We have therefore built this on the same architecture, the same measurement spine and the same central-obligation protocol as the Empowerment paper, so that the sponsor group has the option of approving them as **one initiative with two workstreams and one name — chosen regionally**. Decision 1 in §12.5 is exactly that choice. We would not be disappointed to be overruled, but we would want the overruling to be deliberate.

**The second is the same courtesy we asked for last time.** The regional cards in §6 are working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected. Where a unit has its own diagnostic data, that data supersedes the card and the card is retired (§5.4 of the companion paper applies unchanged). A card returned unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet happened.

One addition on gates: §10 here is materially heavier than in the companion paper, because innovation programmes touch employee-invention statutes, IP assignment, competition law and regulated-market conduct in ways that behaviour programmes do not. Nothing in §3 or §7 should be described to an employee anywhere before §10 has been walked through with Group Legal, Group IP, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Treat the variance between locations as a variance in *conditions*, not in *appetite*. Define four conditions centrally as floors — protected time, an answered route, pre-authorised risk capital, and retained credit — with an alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully be met. Devolve everything else: what counts as an idea, how it is voiced, who convenes, what it is called. Run four instrumented pilots in Year 1, deliberately different in design and identical in instrumentation. Bind the centre to a published response and reversal protocol. And ban idea-volume as a target before anyone thinks of it.**

| | |
|---|---|
| The reframe | Locations do not differ mainly in willingness to innovate. They differ in slack, in distance to someone who can say yes, in the personal cost of a visible failure, and in proximity to a customer whose problem is visible (§2) |
| Global mandate | **Four conditions only** (§3) — protected time; a route from idea to a dated answer; pre-authorised experiment capital; retained credit and attribution. Each a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Definition of "idea", forum design, cadence, language, whether contribution is individual or collective, recognition form, sponsor selection, and the programme's name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one HQ-adjacent, one long-route (three or more layers from a yes), one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** (§7) |
| Principal risk | Not employee reluctance. **Middle-manager delivery exposure** — innovation time comes out of a number someone is measured on (§8.2) |
| Second risk | Innovation theatre: rising idea counts, flat conversion, unchanged latency. Explicitly instrumented as a failure state (§8.5) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published response protocol**: every routed idea receives a named human, a dated answer and a reason within 20 working days; central kill decisions are published with reasoning to the originating audience; response performance is reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Behavioural proxies weighted 75%, survey items 25%. **Idea volume is a diagnostic, never a target** (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Idea submissions +30% or more while funded-experiment conversion is flat and median idea-to-answer latency improves <15% = declared theatre, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$10.6M Year 1, $8.2M Year 2** (illustrative; assumptions §12.1), of which **$4.1M is experiment capital that must actually be spent** and $3.6M is time relief |
| Funding split | Central funds diagnostic, platform, instrumentation, central team, and **100% of experiment capital in Y1** (70% Y2, 40% Y3). Regions fund time relief with a 60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought on **18 March** |
| Owner | Group Chief People Officer with the Group Chief Operating Officer as co-sponsor. We regard the second name as load-bearing (§12.6) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Innovation output across a network tracks the **shortest available route to a yes**, the **recoverable cost of being wrong**, and the **quantity of uncommitted time**, far more closely than it tracks anything cultural. *(Considered practitioner assertion, drawn from our own past programmes and from the pattern in the commissioning brief — not a measured finding in this business. Evidence key at §14.)*

The observation that prompted this paper — "the level of proactive innovation varies significantly by location" — is almost certainly real and almost certainly mis-attributed. Before we accept that some of our offices are more inventive than others, we would want to rule out the duller explanation: that in some offices an idea reaches a decision in nine days and in others it reaches a decision in eleven weeks, or never, and that people have accurately learned which office they are in.

**The specific failure we are trying to avoid** is the one every large company has already run at least once: an idea portal, a hackathon, a poster campaign, and eighteen months later a database of 4,000 suggestions with no owner and a workforce that has learned not to bother. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it burns the credibility a second attempt would need.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The brief describes a culture-and-creativity problem. The available evidence may describe a **routing, slack and downside-cost** problem. Only one of those responds to inspiration.

| Candidate driver of the location variance | What creativity training / campaigns do to it |
|---|---|
| No uncommitted time; every hour is booked to delivery | **Nothing.** The constraint is arithmetic, not attitudinal |
| Route to a decision is long, unnamed, or ends nowhere | Nothing until the route is built and answered (§3.2) |
| A failed experiment is personally career-costly | **Amplifies harm** — you have asked people to volunteer for exposure |
| No money can be spent without a business case that presumes the answer | Nothing — the gate kills the idea before it can be tested |
| Local P&L bears the cost, group bears the benefit | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Ideas travel *to* HQ but never *from* the periphery | Worsens — confirms the periphery's read of its own standing (§11.3) |
| Working-language barrier suppresses half-formed thoughts | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence (§11.1) |
| Customer contact concentrated in a few roles | Partially — but the real fix is contact redistribution (§11.2) |
| Genuine skills gap in framing and testing a hypothesis | **Improves** — this is the one case where training is the right instrument |

Exactly one row in that table is a training problem. We would like to know its weight before committing eight figures.

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Six weeks, no design freeze until it reports.

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Route trace** | Take 25 real ideas already raised in the last 18 months across eight countries. Follow each one forward. Record: who received it, how long to first response, how long to a decision, what the decision was, whether the originator was told. This is the single most informative thing in the diagnostic and it costs almost nothing but persistence |
| **Slack audit** | In twelve units, measure committed vs uncommitted time at three levels. Not self-reported willingness — actual calendar and shift structure |
| **Downside interview** | 50 structured conversations on one question, asked several ways: *what has happened here to someone whose attempt did not work?* Confidentiality-protected, results reported without unit attribution below a threshold of 8 responses |
| **Spend-authority audit** | The smallest sum a named individual can commit to test something, without a business case, at each of four levels in each of eight countries. We expect this number to vary by two orders of magnitude across the network and to explain more than culture does |
| **Language and contact check** | Four sites where the working language is not the local one; plus mapping of which roles have direct customer contact |
| **Cost** | **$340K** |

If the route trace finds median idea-to-decision latency above six weeks anywhere, the Year 1 training envelope should be reduced and redirected to routing and spend authority before any commitment is made. That is the cheapest consequential decision available here.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

*What does the centre give up?*

An innovation programme in which the centre keeps the right to absorb, re-badge, defund or silently ignore what the network produces is not an innovation programme. **§9 sets out four specific, testable, reportable central obligations** — a response service level, published kill reasoning, protection of experiment capital from in-year reallocation, and a reverse-adoption commitment. We would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend §9, not to note it. If §9 is not adopted, our recommendation is to spend the $340K on the diagnostic, publish it, and stop there.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four conditions, stated as floors

Framed as conditions an employee is entitled to find in place, not as behaviours a manager must perform — so that very different local conduct can honour the same floor.

### 3.1 Condition I — protected time exists and is countable
**Floor:** every employee in scope can name a specific, recurring, protected allocation of time available for work not assigned to them, and can point to when they last used it.

The size is regional property. The floor is that it is **named, recurring and countable** — not "when you have a moment," which is the polite form of "never." For deskless and shift populations this will not be individual hours; the honouring forms are shift-overlap windows, rotation into an improvement cell, or a funded relief head (§11.2). For client-billable populations it must be reconciled with utilisation targets *before* launch, or the target quietly wins (§8.2).

**What this is not:** a mandated fixed percentage. We deliberately do not prescribe 15% or 20%. Imported percentages are the most-copied and least-transferable feature of other companies' innovation systems, and in most of our units they would be theatre by week three.

### 3.2 Condition II — there is a route from idea to a dated answer
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available route by which an idea reaches a person empowered to fund, kill or escalate it, and receives from that person **a decision, a date and a reason** within 20 working days.

The route form is entirely local: a written pre-read, a monthly forum, a shift huddle, a skip-level, a named broker role, a queue in the platform, a WhatsApp group with a rota. It need never be a pitch to a room. The **answered** part is the floor.

**The reason is not optional and not a formality.** "No, because we tried this in 2019 and here is what happened" keeps a contributor. "No" alone loses three more ideas that were never sent. Where an idea is killed, the reason is given to the originator and, at the originator's option, to the forum that saw it.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this route is expressly **not** the dissent channel of Empowerment Entitlement II, and expressly **not** any statutory reporting channel. Three separate things, separately named, separately routed, separately governed (§10.4).

### 3.3 Condition III — a bounded amount of risk capital is pre-authorised
**Floor:** in every unit, at least one named individual below the unit head can commit a defined sum to test an idea **without a business case and without an approval step**, within a published experiment perimeter (§3.7).

The sum is regional property and should differ by an order of magnitude between a 40-person branch and a 3,000-person operation. Our working suggestion is that it be large enough to buy a real test and small enough that losing it is unremarkable — in most units, somewhere between $5K and $25K per authorisation, with a quarterly cap.

**A null result is a completed deliverable.** An experiment that runs cleanly and disconfirms the hypothesis has done its job and is reported as done, not as failed. This is the sentence most likely to be nodded at and least likely to be believed, which is why §8.3 instruments it: the proportion of funded experiments with a *documented result of either sign* is a headline metric, and a unit reporting a 95% success rate is reporting that it is not experimenting.

### 3.4 Condition IV — the contributor stays attached
**Floor:** an idea that is adopted carries, in the record and in the telling, the name of the person or team that originated it; and the originator has a **right of first refusal** to be involved in taking it forward.

*Right of first refusal*, not obligation. Some contributors want the work; some want the credit and their existing job; some — in several regions, most — want the credit to attach to their team rather than to themselves. All three are honoured forms. What is not honoured is an idea arriving at the centre from a branch and re-emerging as a group initiative with no branch in it. That has happened in this company and people remember (§11.3).

**Statutory overlay:** in Germany and several other jurisdictions, employee inventions carry a *statutory* compensation entitlement that is not ours to design around, and attribution has legal as well as cultural weight (§10.2). Condition IV is drafted to sit above those floors, never below them.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
What counts as an idea. Whether contribution is framed individually or collectively. Forum design, cadence, symbolism, recognition form, whether recognition is public or private, sponsor selection, tooling, and the programme's name. **We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name**, for the reasons given in the companion paper.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process

Identical in machinery to the companion paper, and deliberately so — one register, one approver, one review.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, regulatory prohibition, or structural impossibility. Not difficulty. Not cost. Not discomfort |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the nearest form the unit *can* honour, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group CPO**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal; Group IP added where Condition IV is engaged |
| Duration | 12 months, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Internally published register, shared with the empowerment register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | Accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect **six to ten** in Year 1 — more than the companion paper, because the legal surface here is wider — and would be actively suspicious of zero |

### 3.7 The experiment perimeter (the thing that makes Condition III safe)

Pre-authorised capital without a perimeter is how a well-run company acquires a regulatory finding. Every unit publishes, before its first experiment, a one-page perimeter stating what may be tried without further approval. Our proposed default, to be adapted regionally:

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |

# Critique — Innovation Capacity & Experimentation Initiative v1.0

## 1. The disqualifying issue first

**The document is incomplete.** It terminates mid-sentence in §3.7 ("internal process changes; simulations and"). Sections §4 through §14 do not exist, yet the paper cross-references them 40+ times as though they carry the argument. Specifically missing:

- **§9 — the central obligations protocol.** §2.3 states: *"If §9 is not adopted, our recommendation is to spend the $340K on the diagnostic, publish it, and stop there."* The paper makes §9 the go/no-go condition of the entire investment and then does not write it. This is the single most consequential omission.
- **§12.5 — the three decisions requested.** The cover note says "Decision 1 in §12.5 is exactly that choice" (merge vs. two programmes). No decisions are enumerated anywhere. A paper whose stated purpose is "for decision at the sponsor group meeting of 18 March" contains no decisions.
- **§8 (measurement and failure states), §7 (pilot design), §10 (legal gates — which the cover note calls "materially heavier" than the companion), §11 (language, deskless, periphery), §12.1 (cost assumptions), §14 (evidence key).**

A sponsor group cannot act on this. Everything below assumes the missing sections will be written and is directed at the reasoning that *is* visible.

## 2. Fit to the original request

The request was for **strategies to foster innovation, creativity and risk-taking across international offices**. The paper answers a narrower question — *how to govern and instrument an innovation programme* — and answers it well. But it under-serves three parts of the brief:

- **"Responsive to market changes"** is barely addressed. Customer contact appears as one row in the §2.1 table and one line in the diagnostic. There is no market-sensing design, no mechanism converting a customer signal in Jakarta into an offer change, no cycle-time metric from external signal to internal response. For a company whose stated goal is market responsiveness, this is a structural gap, not a detail.
- **Cross-border diffusion is missing.** The highest-value asset of a 14-region network is that a validated experiment in one market can be transplanted to eleven others. "Reverse adoption" appears once, as a bullet in §2.3, and is never designed. No portfolio view, no scaling gate, no adopt-or-explain mechanism, no cross-region visibility of what is being tested where. This should be a fifth condition or a named workstream.
- **Idea quality and strategic focus are absent.** The paper devolves "what counts as an idea" entirely. Combined with no challenge-framing mechanism, the predictable output is the 4,000-suggestion cafeteria database the paper itself invokes as the nightmare scenario. The standard, evidenced remedy — leadership-issued *challenge statements* that give creativity a target — is conspicuously not proposed.

Also absent, and legitimately within scope: hiring/onboarding for experimentation, an internal practitioner network (ambassadors/brokers), external ecosystem access (customers, startups, universities), and asynchronous collaboration design across time zones — a specifically *international* constraint the paper never mentions.

## 3. Logic and analytic errors

1. **The failure test is one-directional and gameable.** "+30% submissions with flat conversion and <15% latency improvement = theatre." A unit can pass simply by suppressing submissions. And the test is keyed to volume — the very metric the paper insists is "never a target." Needs a symmetric formulation anchored on conversion, latency and *deployed* outcomes, with a volume-collapse trigger as a second failure state.

2. **The 20-working-day SLA is unfunded and uncapacitied.** No volume forecast, no handling-time estimate, no broker FTE calculation, no queue design. The most probable failure of this programme is SLA breach in month four, which converts the centre's flagship commitment into its most visible broken promise. Add a capacity model and an explicit rule: *throttle intake before breaking the answer.*

3. **"$4.1M of experiment capital that must actually be spent"** installs a spend target — the identical pathology to an idea-volume target, and it will produce make-work experiments. Reframe: capital is *protected and available*; deployment rate is a **diagnostic** (low deployment signals a routing failure, not a spending failure), never a target.

4. **Condition III collides with financial control and no one has been asked.** "A named individual below unit head can commit $5K–$25K without a business case and without an approval step" touches delegation-of-authority, segregation of duties, SOX-equivalent controls, anti-bribery and procurement policy. The **CFO, Group Internal Audit and Group Procurement do not appear anywhere** in the sponsor, circulation or countersignature lists. This is the most likely source of a late, fatal veto. Also internally inconsistent: the "perimeter" *is* an approval construct, so "no approval step" is imprecise — say "pre-approved within a published perimeter."

5. **Diagnostic sample sizes do not support the claims made of them.** 25 ideas across 8 countries is ~3 per country — insufficient to estimate a latency distribution, let alone compare units. It is also survivorship-biased: it can only trace ideas someone remembers raising, systematically excluding the population that matters most (ideas never submitted). Widen substantially, pull from systems rather than memory, and add explicit probing for suppression.

6. **The downside-interview threshold is arithmetically self-defeating.** 50 interviews, results suppressed below 8 responses per unit — across eight countries and multiple levels, almost no unit will clear the threshold. Either concentrate the sample in fewer units or accept region-level reporting and say so.

7. **"Exactly one row in that table is a training problem"** is rhetorically satisfying and factually wrong by the paper's own table: the customer-contact row is marked "Partially." Small, but it is exactly the kind of overreach a CFO catches and then discounts the rest.

8. **No comparison design.** Four pilots with no matched control or stepped-wedge sequencing means any Year 1 improvement is unattributable. Given that the paper's whole ethic is instrumentation over assertion, this is an inconsistency. Propose matched non-pilot units or staggered start dates.

9. **Null-result incentive is gameable.** "A 95% success rate means you are not experimenting" invites trivial or deliberately doomed tests. Require **pre-registration** of hypothesis, decision rule and success criterion before capital release; measure the proportion of experiments whose pre-registered decision rule was actually followed.

10. **Condition IV (named attribution) conflicts with jurisdictions the paper itself cites.** Individual-performance visibility is a works-council and data-protection matter in Germany and the Netherlands; the paper simultaneously notes that several regions prefer collective framing. The resolution ("all three forms are honoured") is asserted, not designed. Also, "right of first refusal to be involved" has resourcing and job-content consequences that will interest works councils.

## 4. Consistency with the companion paper

The paper claims "the same architecture, the same measurement spine." It is not the same:

- **Weighting differs (70/30 vs 75/25)** with no stated reason. Either reconcile or explain; a "common spine" that differs in its first parameter is not common.
- **Acquiescence correction** (companion §8.3) is not mentioned here. Cross-region comparison will be invalid without it.
- **Pilot selection axes differ.** Four pilots there, four here, on different criteria. If merged, are these four units or eight? Unresolved, and it drives cost.
- **Two diagnostics** ($310K/5 weeks; $340K/6 weeks), both in eight countries, both interviewing overlapping populations (60 + 50 conversations). Respondent fatigue plus duplicated field cost. Merge into one instrument.
- **Combined ask is $24.8M in Year 1** across two papers landing at one meeting. No combined envelope, no de-duplication of platform, instrumentation, central team and programme management. **The paper recommends merger as Decision 1 and then fails to price the merged option** — so the sponsor group is asked to choose between a costed standalone and an uncosted merger. Present the merged design as the base case with a single budget, savings quantified, and the two-programme option as the alternative.
- **Six decisions on one agenda** (three there, three here) is not addressed.

## 5. Business case

There is no benefit case. $18.8M over two years is requested with no hypothesis about what it returns — no target for time-to-market, revenue from experiments, cost savings from process innovations, or market-response cycle time. The paper is admirably rigorous about *cost* and *failure*, and silent on *value*. Any competent sponsor group will stop at this. Add a benefits section with explicit, falsifiable targets and a break-even threshold, even if ranged and clearly labelled as judgement.

## 6. Style and credibility

- **Fabricated institutional memory.** "That has happened in this company and people remember" (§3.4) is presented as fact with no source. The paper is otherwise scrupulous about its evidence key; this line, and several like it, breach that discipline.
- **Mannerism.** "We would gently ask," "We would not be disappointed to be overruled," "One note only, and then the substance." Once, distinctive. Repeatedly, and duplicated verbatim from the companion paper, it reads as house template and dilutes force. The credibility sentence ("worse than no initiative, because it burns the credibility a second attempt would need") is a near word-for-word lift.
- **Structural contradiction.** The paper opens by arguing this should not be a second programme, then delivers a complete second programme with its own budget, owner, diagnostic, pilots and decisions. Argue one thing, structure the other, and readers trust neither.
- **Missing:** timeline/critical path, RACI, scope carry-forward of the Russia/Belarus exclusion, treatment of JVs/franchises/contractors, and a one-page executive summary that survives being read alone.

## 7. What is genuinely strong and must survive revision

The reframe from *appetite* to *conditions* (slack, route length, downside cost, customer proximity) is the paper's best contribution and is correct. The **route trace** is the highest-yield-per-dollar diagnostic in either document. The **spend-authority audit** — expecting two orders of magnitude of variance — is likely to explain more than any culture finding. Idea volume as diagnostic-not-target, the three-way firewall between idea route / dissent channel / statutory reporting, the employee-invention statutory overlay, the refusal to import a 15% rule, and naming middle-manager delivery exposure as the principal risk are all correct and unusually well judged.

## 8. Priority fixes

1. Complete §§4–14; write §9 first, since the paper conditions the investment on it.
2. Enumerate the three decisions and reconcile them with the companion's three.
3. Price the merged option as the base case; merge the two diagnostics into one.
4. Add a benefits case with falsifiable targets.
5. Bring CFO, Internal Audit and Procurement into Condition III design before circulation.
6. Add a capacity model behind the 20-day SLA and a throttle rule.
7. Fix the failure test (symmetric, conversion-anchored); reframe experiment capital as available-not-spent.
8. Add the two missing design elements the brief actually asked for: **challenge-framing / strategic focus**, and **cross-border scaling of validated experiments**.
9. Add a comparison design (matched units or stepped wedge).
10. Strip the unsourced institutional-memory claims or move them under the evidence key.

**Overall Assessment: MAJOR_REVISIONS**
[END QUALITY FEEDBACK]

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Innovation output across a network tracks the **shortest available route to a yes**, the **recoverable cost of being wrong**, and the **quantity of uncommitted time**, far more closely than it tracks anything cultural. *(Considered practitioner assertion, drawn from our own past programmes and from the pattern in the commissioning brief — not a measured finding in this business. Evidence key at §14.)*

The observation that prompted this paper — "the level of proactive innovation varies significantly by location" — is almost certainly real and almost certainly mis-attributed. Before we accept that some of our offices are more inventive than others, we would want to rule out the duller explanation: that in some offices an idea reaches a decision in nine days and in others it reaches a decision in eleven weeks, or never, and that people have accurately learned which office they are in.

**The specific failure we are trying to avoid** is the one every large company has already run at least once: an idea portal, a hackathon, a poster campaign, and eighteen months later a database of 4,000 suggestions with no owner and a workforce that has learned not to bother. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it burns the credibility a second attempt would need.

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The brief describes a culture-and-creativity problem. The available evidence may describe a **routing, slack and downside-cost** problem. Only one of those responds to inspiration.

| Candidate driver of the location variance | What creativity training / campaigns do to it |
|---|---|
| No uncommitted time; every hour is booked to delivery | **Nothing.** The constraint is arithmetic, not attitudinal |
| Route to a decision is long, unnamed, or ends nowhere | Nothing until the route is built and answered (§3.2) |
| A failed experiment is personally career-costly | **Amplifies harm** — you have asked people to volunteer for exposure |
| No money can be spent without a business case that presumes the answer | Nothing — the gate kills the idea before it can be tested |

| Working-language barrier suppresses half-formed thoughts | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence (§11.1) |

| Genuine skills gap in framing and testing a hypothesis | **Improves** — this is the one case where training is the right instrument |

Exactly one row in that table is a training problem. We would like to know its weight before committing eight figures.

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Six weeks, no design freeze until it reports.

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Route trace** | Take 25 real ideas already raised in the last 18 months across eight countries. Follow each one forward. Record: who received it, how long to first response, how long to a decision, what the decision was, whether the originator was told. This is the single most informative thing in the diagnostic and it costs almost nothing but persistence |
| **Slack audit** | In twelve units, measure committed vs uncommitted time at three levels. Not self-reported willingness — actual calendar and shift structure |
| **Downside interview** | 50 structured conversations on one question, asked several ways: *what has happened here to someone whose attempt did not work?* Confidentiality-protected, results reported without unit attribution below a threshold of 8 responses |
| **Spend-authority audit** | The smallest sum a named individual can commit to test something, without a business case, at each of four levels in each of eight countries. We expect this number to vary by two orders of magnitude across the network and to explain more than culture does |
| **Language and contact check** | Four sites where the working language is not the local one; plus mapping of which roles have direct customer contact |
| **Cost** | **$340K** |

If the route trace finds median idea-to-decision latency above six weeks anywhere, the Year 1 training envelope should be reduced and redirected to routing and spend authority before any commitment is made. That is the cheapest consequential decision available here.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

*What does the centre give up?*

An innovation programme in which the centre keeps the right to absorb, re-badge, defund or silently ignore what the network produces is not an innovation programme. **§9 sets out four specific, testable, reportable central obligations** — a response service level, published kill reasoning, protection of experiment capital from in-year reallocation, and a reverse-adoption commitment. We would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend §9, not to note it. If §9 is not adopted, our recommendation is to spend the $340K on the diagnostic, publish it, and stop there.

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four conditions, stated as floors

Framed as conditions an employee is entitled to find in place, not as behaviours a manager must perform — so that very different local conduct can honour the same floor.

### 3.1 Condition I — protected time exists and is countable
**Floor:** every employee in scope can name a specific, recurring, protected allocation of time available for work not assigned to them, and can point to when they last used it.

The size is regional property. The floor is that it is **named, recurring and countable** — not "when you have a moment," which is the polite form of "never." For deskless and shift populations this will not be individual hours; the honouring forms are shift-overlap windows, rotation into an improvement cell, or a funded relief head (§11.2). For client-billable populations it must be reconciled with utilisation targets *before* launch, or the target quietly wins (§8.2).

**What this is not:** a mandated fixed percentage. We deliberately do not prescribe 15% or 20%. Imported percentages are the most-copied and least-transferable feature of other companies' innovation systems, and in most of our units they would be theatre by week three.

### 3.2 Condition II — there is a route from idea to a dated answer
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available route by which an idea reaches a person empowered to fund, kill or escalate it, and receives from that person **a decision, a date and a reason** within 20 working days.

The route form is entirely local: a written pre-read, a monthly forum, a shift huddle, a skip-level, a named broker role, a queue in the platform, a WhatsApp group with a rota. It need never be a pitch to a room. The **answered** part is the floor.

**The reason is not optional and not a formality.** "No, because we tried this in 2019 and here is what happened" keeps a contributor. "No" alone loses three more ideas that were never sent. Where an idea is killed, the reason is given to the originator and, at the originator's option, to the forum that saw it.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this route is expressly **not** the dissent channel of Empowerment Entitlement II, and expressly **not** any statutory reporting channel. Three separate things, separately named, separately routed, separately governed (§10.4).

### 3.3 Condition III — a bounded amount of risk capital is pre-authorised
**Floor:** in every unit, at least one named individual below the unit head can commit a defined sum to test an idea **without a business case and without an approval step**, within a published experiment perimeter (§3.7).

The sum is regional property and should differ by an order of magnitude between a 40-person branch and a 3,000-person operation. Our working suggestion is that it be large enough to buy a real test and small enough that losing it is unremarkable — in most units, somewhere between $5K and $25K per authorisation, with a quarterly cap.

**A null result is a completed deliverable.** An experiment that runs cleanly and disconfirms the hypothesis has done its job and is reported as done, not as failed. This is the sentence most likely to be nodded at and least likely to be believed, which is why §8.3 instruments it: the proportion of funded experiments with a *documented result of either sign* is a headline metric, and a unit reporting a 95% success rate is reporting that it is not experimenting.

### 3.4 Condition IV — the contributor stays attached
**Floor:** an idea that is adopted carries, in the record and in the telling, the name of the person or team that originated it; and the originator has a **right of first refusal** to be involved in taking it forward.

*Right of first refusal*, not obligation. Some contributors want the work; some want the credit and their existing job; some — in several regions, most — want the credit to attach to their team rather than to themselves. All three are honoured forms. What is not honoured is an idea arriving at the centre from a branch and re-emerging as a group initiative with no branch in it. That has happened in this company and people remember (§11.3).

**Statutory overlay:** in Germany and several other jurisdictions, employee inventions carry a *statutory* compensation entitlement that is not ours to design around, and attribution has legal as well as cultural weight (§10.2). Condition IV is drafted to sit above those floors, never below them.

What counts as an idea. Whether contribution is framed individually or collectively. Forum design, cadence, symbolism, recognition form, whether recognition is public or private, sponsor selection, tooling, and the programme's name. **We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name**, for the reasons given in the companion paper.

## 3. Logic and analytic errors

1. **The failure test is one-directional and gameable.** "+30% submissions with flat conversion and <15% latency improvement = theatre." A unit can pass simply by suppressing submissions. And the test is keyed to volume — the very metric the paper insists is "never a target." Needs a symmetric formulation anchored on conversion, latency and *deployed* outcomes, with a volume-collapse trigger as a second failure state.

2. **The 20-working-day SLA is unfunded and uncapacitied.** No volume forecast, no handling-time estimate, no broker FTE calculation, no queue design. The most probable failure of this programme is SLA breach in month four, which converts the centre's flagship commitment into its most visible broken promise. Add a capacity model and an explicit rule: *throttle intake before breaking the answer.*

3. **"$4.1M of experiment capital that must actually be spent"** installs a spend target — the identical pathology to an idea-volume target, and it will produce make-work experiments. Reframe: capital is *protected and available*; deployment rate is a **diagnostic** (low deployment signals a routing failure, not a spending failure), never a target.

4. **Condition III collides with financial control and no one has been asked.** "A named individual below unit head can commit $5K–$25K without a business case and without an approval step" touches delegation-of-authority, segregation of duties, SOX-equivalent controls, anti-bribery and procurement policy. The **CFO, Group Internal Audit and Group Procurement do not appear anywhere** in the sponsor, circulation or countersignature lists. This is the most likely source of a late, fatal veto. Also internally inconsistent: the "perimeter" *is* an approval construct, so "no approval step" is imprecise — say "pre-approved within a published perimeter."

5. **Diagnostic sample sizes do not support the claims made of them.** 25 ideas across 8 countries is ~3 per country — insufficient to estimate a latency distribution, let alone compare units. It is also survivorship-biased: it can only trace ideas someone remembers raising, systematically excluding the population that matters most (ideas never submitted). Widen substantially, pull from systems rather than memory, and add explicit probing for suppression.

6. **The downside-interview threshold is arithmetically self-defeating.** 50 interviews, results suppressed below 8 responses per unit — across eight countries and multiple levels, almost no unit will clear the threshold. Either concentrate the sample in fewer units or accept region-level reporting and say so.

7. **"Exactly one row in that table is a training problem"** is rhetorically satisfying and factually wrong by the paper's own table: the customer-contact row is marked "Partially." Small, but it is exactly the kind of overreach a CFO catches and then discounts the rest.

8. **No comparison design.** Four pilots with no matched control or stepped-wedge sequencing means any Year 1 improvement is unattributable. Given that the paper's whole ethic is instrumentation over assertion, this is an inconsistency. Propose matched non-pilot units or staggered start dates.

9. **Null-result incentive is gameable.** "A 95% success rate means you are not experimenting" invites trivial or deliberately doomed tests. Require **pre-registration** of hypothesis, decision rule and success criterion before capital release; measure the proportion of experiments whose pre-registered decision rule was actually followed.

10. **Condition IV (named attribution) conflicts with jurisdictions the paper itself cites.** Individual-performance visibility is a works-council and data-protection matter in Germany and the Netherlands; the paper simultaneously notes that several regions prefer collective framing. The resolution ("all three forms are honoured") is asserted, not designed. Also, "right of first refusal to be involved" has resourcing and job-content consequences that will interest works councils.
